topIssues.title: kona-node: finalized head does not leave genesis after an EL datadir wipe
topIssues.author: einar-oplabs
topIssues.body:
**Claude:** After an op-reth follower's datadir is wiped under a kona-node that kept its heads, kona-node resyncs the unsafe and safe heads but its finalized head does not reliably leave genesis.

Observed in `TestFollowerResyncsFromScratchUnderConsensusClientThatKeptItsHeads/el_sync` (`op-acceptance-tests/tests/op_reth_stale_forkchoice`, #23440) under `DEVSTACK_L2CL_KIND=kona-node`, CircleCI job 5705185:

- The first consolidation after the wipe finds no block in the empty engine (``Received `None` block for 186``, `Consolidate(MissingUnsafeL2Block(186))`) and resets. The reset reads the wiped engine's labels (`unsafe=0 safe=0 finalized=0`), the sync-start safe search walks back to genesis, and derivation restarts at L1 genesis.
- Whenever the derived safe head catches up with the engine's canonical tip while the gossip-fed unsafe head is ahead, the next consolidation finds `None` again and resets again; each reset clears the finalization queue (`L2Finalizer::clear` on `Signal::Reset`).
- A finalize task that landed after a reset hit `FinalizeTaskError::BlockNotSafe`, which kona-node treats as critical: `Failed to start rollup node service: EngineTask(Finalize(BlockNotSafe))`. The finalized wait then failed with `expected head for label=finalized to advance to target=59, but got current=0`.

op-node passes the same scenario. Note for whoever picks this up: in the same CI log the follower's op-reth answered null by number for block 348 while it had received payload 361, so the EL's behaviour below its highest payload is worth checking too.

The finalized check in that test cell is skipped under kona-node naming this issue.

topIssues.title: flaky test: `TestSuperInvalidateUnsafeProposal` and `TestSuperInvalidateCorrectProposalFutureBlock` hang in batcher stop
topIssues.author: ajsutton
topIssues.body:
**Claude:** I made this report from the CI logs.

`op-e2e-cannon-tests-super` in `develop-fault-proofs` hung in 3 of its last 48 runs. Each time, CircleCI stopped the job after 90 minutes with no output.

| Job | Hung subtest |
|---|---|
| [5941119](https://app.circleci.com/jobs/gh/ethereum-optimism/optimism/5941119) | `TestSuperInvalidateUnsafeProposal/Defend-mt-cannon-next` |
| [5922649](https://app.circleci.com/jobs/gh/ethereum-optimism/optimism/5922649) | `TestSuperInvalidateUnsafeProposal/Defend-mt-cannon-next` |
| [5919990](https://app.circleci.com/jobs/gh/ethereum-optimism/optimism/5919990) | `TestSuperInvalidateCorrectProposalFutureBlock/Defend-mt-cannon-next` |

Both tests stop each batcher with `sys.Batcher(id).Stop(ctx)` and `context.Background()`. In the hung subtest, the test writes no output after its start. After the stop, the batcher logs `Receipt retrieval failed ... err="client is closed"` every 50 ms until CircleCI stops the job. The hung subtest log has about 243,000 of these lines. Passing subtests of the same tests log 0 to 80 of these lines and then continue.

The batcher `Stop` call probably waits for a transaction receipt after it closes its L1 client. That wait has no end. A fix agent will confirm the cause.

topIssues.title: kona: cannot derive a chain whose L1 is an OP Stack chain
topIssues.author: sebastianst
topIssues.body:
kona cannot derive a chain whose L1 is itself an OP Stack chain (an L3). op-node supports that setup, and the derivation spec [lists the deposit type](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/specs/blob/48504e5b0fdcd0f01a2c0b522e91f699cfc95b71/specs/protocol/derivation.md?plain=1#L507-L508) among the batcher transaction types "to support force-inclusion of batcher transactions on nested OP Stack chains".

This is from reading the code; it was not run against an OP Stack L1.

## Where it stops

Every block of an OP Stack L1 starts with an L1-info deposit (type `0x7E`) and can hold post-exec transactions (`0x7D`). kona reads L1 blocks with alloy's Ethereum transaction envelope, which has neither:

- **kona-node:** [`AlloyChainProvider::block_info_and_transactions_by_hash`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/f0d907fd862acb2fecd354a0cfe6fbe9c7a47a2a/rust/kona/crates/providers/providers-alloy/src/chain_provider.rs#L764-L805) fetches the full block through an Ethereum-network provider and maps it to `Vec<TxEnvelope>`, so deserializing the block fails on the first transaction.
- **kona-client:** [`OracleL1ChainProvider`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/f0d907fd862acb2fecd354a0cfe6fbe9c7a47a2a/rust/kona/crates/proof/proof/src/l1/chain_provider.rs#L139-L148) decodes each transaction of the trie with `TxEnvelope::decode_2718`, which fails on `0x7E`.
- **Data sources:** even with a decodable envelope, the [calldata source](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/f0d907fd862acb2fecd354a0cfe6fbe9c7a47a2a/rust/kona/crates/protocol/derive/src/sources/calldata.rs#L46-L54) and the [blob source](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/f0d907fd862acb2fecd354a0cfe6fbe9c7a47a2a/rust/kona/crates/protocol/derive/src/sources/blobs.rs#L50-L66) only consider legacy, EIP-2930, EIP-1559 and EIP-4844 transactions, so a batcher transaction that was force-included as a deposit is ignored.

Not checked: L1 receipts, which kona also decodes with Ethereum types and which hold deposit receipts on an OP Stack L1.

## What op-node does

op-node reads the L1 block's transactions as EIP-2718 bytes and decodes each by its class (#24281): a deposit to the batch inbox whose `From` is the batcher address is a batcher transaction, since a deposit carries its sender instead of a signature; a post-exec transaction never is; every other transaction goes through the signature check.

## To decide

- Should kona support an OP Stack L1? If yes, its L1 providers need a transaction type that covers the OP transaction types, and the data sources need the deposit rule above.
- If not, the spec and op-node keep a rule that the Rust stack does not implement, and that should be stated somewhere an L3 operator finds it.

The spec text itself needs a small fix either way: it says the sender is "recovered from the transaction signature", which does not apply to a deposit.

topIssues.title: supernode: Resolve "Optimistic" function name conflicts
topIssues.author: axelKingsley
topIssues.body:
Currently there is some overloaded meaning in the term "Optimistic", which differs when there is a replacement block. For posterity:

Verified: The block is a valid block, and will be a replacement block if not. An invalid block will never be verified.

Optimistic: The block which would be on the chain if no replacements occurred. Will be the valid OR invalid block, but never a replacement block.
Technically, Optimistic blocks are uncles of the chain when they represent the replaced block. So there is no forward progression of a replaced block as a chain.

Local: The chain currently known to the derivation pipeline. At-tip, blocks may be Verified, Invalid, or Replaced (because we may be actively verifying the chain by protocol rules), but behind some point the chain is always Verified.

In updating Superroots to use the Denylist as preference for Optimistic Outputs, I noticed we also have `OptimisticAt` which is used in more places. At present I am not sure if that method is meant to reference the chain by Optimistic or Local concept. This task is to capture some investigation of the intent of callers so we can correctly amend the function names or usages.

topPRs.title: op-reth!: let a binary embed op-reth with overrides
topPRs.author: joshklop
topPRs.body:
Step 3 of making op-reth-premium a thin "op-reth plus subblocks" wrapper. This PR is stacked on #24270.

Today premium copies op-reth's startup and launch code and defines its own node types, so changes to op-reth's launch never reach it. This PR lets a binary embed op-reth instead, the way tempo's `tempo_main_with(TempoOverrides)` works.

- **First commit:** `op_reth::main_with(OpRethOverrides)` runs op-reth with three additions:
  - extra `node` arguments, flattened after op-reth's own in `OpRethArgs`;
  - the embedder's version metadata;
  - one `customize` step. It gets the node config, the extra arguments and the `OpNode` op-reth built. It returns the node to launch, plus two hooks with concrete types: an RPC extension and an on-started hook.
- **Second commit:** `OpNode::with_pool` / `with_payload` return a `CustomOpNode`, with a replaced pool builder or payload service. `CustomOpNode` keeps its `OpNode` private, so changing a config field afterwards can't split the components from the add-ons.

These hooks are exactly the ones premium uses. I rewrote premium on this branch as a check, kept as a local, unpushed commit for the final premium PR:
- the rewrite deletes `PremiumOpNode`, `PremiumStandardSdmOpNode`, `SdmStandardPayloadServiceBuilder` and `launch_and_await_exit`;
- a small enum chooses between the subblocks and SDM-standard payload services;
- it is +282/−465 lines, excluding lockfiles;
- its clippy, unit tests (593) and in-process node tests (95) pass;
- the API needed no premium special cases.

**Effect on op-reth:** none at runtime. The `node` command line is unchanged; a test compares its help with the `Cli<RollupArgs>` one that the CLI snapshot pins. Startup order and logs are unchanged. One thing differs: a failure to install the version metadata now stops op-reth instead of printing a warning. That can only happen if another caller claimed the metadata first.

**Library users:** `launch_node` takes a third argument, `OpLaunchHooks`. Pass `OpLaunchHooks::default()` to keep today's behaviour.

**Room for kona (#23826):** op-reth's own `node` arguments go in `OpRethArgs`. A future that runs alongside the node can race `launch` in `main_with`, or go on `OpLaunchHooks`.

### Compile memory

op-reth's own launch stays non-generic, because a generic launch compiles in its caller's crate. Only a `CustomOpNode` launches through the generic `LaunchOpNode`, which compiles in the embedder's crate.

I measured the peak RSS of each rustc/rustdoc process with a `RUSTC_WRAPPER`/`RUSTDOC` wrapper that reads `getrusage`, on an M-series Mac. "Before" is #24270's head, `2bf0e403ab`. Wall times are noisy, because other builds were running on the machine.

`cargo build --release -p op-reth --bin op-reth` (the binary's own feature set):

| rustc process | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `op-reth` bin | 9.82 GiB | 7.98 GiB |
| `op-reth` lib | 0.12 GiB | 5.79 GiB |
| `reth-optimism-node` lib | 5.43 GiB | 5.54 GiB |

`reth-optimism-node --all-features`, the case that ran the 16 GB executor out of memory before (#20100, #20337, #19935):

| rustc process | debug before → after | release before → after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| lib (`cargo build`) | 12.23 → 13.63 GiB | 6.85 → 6.93 GiB |
| lib unit tests (`cargo test --no-run`) | 9.01 → 10.56 GiB | 6.53 → 7.06 GiB |
| `tests/it` binary | 7.60 → 7.49 GiB | 10.76 → 11.86 GiB |
| doctests (`cargo test --doc`) | 1.36 → 1.36 GiB | 4.33 → 4.21 GiB |

What I infer:
- **The op-reth binary's peak falls.** The startup code moved from the bin to the new lib, so the two peaks no longer stack.
- **This PR raises `reth-optimism-node`'s `--all-features` peak by about 1.1–1.6 GiB.** That covers the debug lib, the debug unit tests and the release `tests/it` binary. These builds run on the 32 GB executor, but this works against #19935.
- **Likely cause (unverified):** the generic `CustomOpNode` path adds a layer of node types and impls that rustc compiles in the same process as the launch.
- **Follow-up:** the planned launcher-crate PR, stacked on this one, moves the launch out of `reth-optimism-node` and should take this back out. I did not work around it here.

### Behaviour changes for premium

There is no premium PR yet, so these are listed here.

- **Standard SDM path pool:** it now installs the policy pool instead of the stock pool, because one node type needs one pool type. Rules are rejected on that path, so the ruleset stays empty. This relies on `PremiumConfig::rules_enabled`'s documented claim that an empty-ruleset policy pool admits and orders like the stock pool.
- **Launch:** premium launches through op-reth's launch, which adds:
  - reth's debug launcher, which stays inert because premium still rejects `--dev`, `--debug.rpc-consensus-url` and `--debug.etherscan`;
  - the runtime state-masking guard;
  - the storage-v1 warning;
  - one more "Launching node" log line.
- **Startup:** op-reth's startup runs first:
  - the SIGSEGV handler;
  - `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` when unset;
  - the `--testing.sdm-fixed-policy` registry rejection and its TEST-ONLY warning;
  - the registry block-time default, which premium already applied.

  When both sides fail, op-reth's error comes first.
- **Build:** premium's `payload` crate compiles one launch instead of two.

These are unchanged, but now need a decision:
- `--proofs-history` is still ignored on the subblocks path and rejected without subblocks, although op-reth's launch could now serve it on both.
- The debug-launcher flags are still rejected.
- `--testing.sdm-fixed-policy` is accepted and logged as enabled, but neither premium payload service applies it.
- Premium declares no global allocator, so it runs on the system allocator.

### Reviews

- **Stale config:** `rust-code-reviewer` and `deletion-reviewer` both flagged that the first version of the second commit built the pool and payload service once, from public fields that could still change. The `CustomOpNode` wrapper replaces that design.
- I applied their other findings, except:
  - `+ OpNodeTypes` on the `LaunchOpNode` and `DebugNode` bounds stays. Without it the associated types don't normalize: removing it gives 88 errors.
  - the CLI snapshot test still uses `Cli<RollupArgs>`. `reth-optimism-cli` can't depend on `op-reth`, so the help-equality test lives in `op-reth`.

topPRs.title: op-chain-ops: add sequencer-recovery for interop reorg stalls
topPRs.author: karlfloersch
topPRs.body:
After a supernode invalidates a block that holds an invalid executing message, the conductor cluster can stop sequencing until an operator intervenes. The sequencers' op-nodes move to the supernode's deposit-only replacement, but every conductor's raft log still holds the payload committed before the reorg. Each conductor that becomes leader fails `unsafe head mismatch`, does not start its sequencer and transfers leadership. Leadership then loops through the cluster and no blocks are produced.

`sequencer-recovery` gives operators a health check and a scripted restart for this state. It reads the op-conductor-ops config that netchef renders, plus the chain's supernode RPC. `status` separates problems that stop sequencing from per-node problems that need a resync. `recover` prints the plan, and with `--execute` runs it. The README in `op-chain-ops/cmd/sequencer-recovery` has the runbook.

**Testing on a devnet.** On a two-chain interop devnet (`dev/int-reorg-0`, permissive interop filter, three sequencers per chain under op-conductor, light nodes following three supernodes), invalid executing messages reproduced the stall repeatedly. The tool recovered it each time, both by hand and from an automatic loop. Running it unattended found four problems, now fixed and covered by tests:

- A failed step left every conductor paused. The resume steps now run as cleanup after any failure.
- Stopping a sequencer that had already stopped, during the conductor's own leadership handoff, aborted the run. Now it does not.
- Supernode or proxyd-cl errors during a supernode rewind made active sequencers look inactive and triggered false recoveries. A failed supernode comparison is now a per-node problem only.
- Resuming the conductors as soon as the restarted leader had built two blocks let its own conductor judge it unhealthy, because catch-up blocks carry old timestamps. Leadership then moved to a standby without those blocks and the stall returned. The plan now waits until the leader's head is within `--caught-up-within` (default 10s) of wall-clock time.

**Limitations.**
- It does not repair a node whose execution client cannot backfill the gap after a reorg.
- It does not repair a light op-node that cannot reach the supernode's replacement block because its execution client lacks that block.
- It assumes the sequencer IDs in the config are the raft server IDs. The netchef-rendered config satisfies this.

The root cause is in op-conductor. A leader should accept its op-node's unsafe head when that head is on the supernode-verified chain, rather than insist on the stale raft payload. This tool is the recovery procedure until that change lands.

**Review status.** The review agents in `.claude/agents` (`go-code-reviewer`) have not been run on this draft yet. `go test ./op-chain-ops/sequencerrecovery/...` passes, and the repo's custom golangci-lint reports 0 issues on the new packages.

topPRs.title: op-chain-ops: add interop reorg stress tooling
topPRs.author: karlfloersch
topPRs.body:
Adds two op-chain-ops tools for stress-testing interop invalidation on a devnet whose interop filter lets invalid executing messages through, such as one running the permissive filter mock.

- `interop-safety-check` independently re-validates every `CrossL2Inbox` executing message up to each op-supernode's cross-safe head against the initiating log, using that supernode's own ELs. It also checks that all supernodes agree on the cross-safe chain, that given invalidated transactions are gone, that replaced blocks hold only deposits, and that cross-safe keeps advancing. It answers the main safety question of an invalidation test, whether an invalid message ever reaches cross-safe, without trusting any supernode's decision.
- `interop-smoke invalid-spam` sends invalid executing messages back to back on both chains, without waiting for reorgs, so nearly every batch has to be invalidated. The existing `invalid-message` subcommand waits for each reorg, which limits it to a few invalidations per run.

On the two-chain int-reorg-0 devnet (three supernodes, three conductor-managed sequencers per chain), the safety check ran every 30s through repeated single, multi-block and chained invalidations. It found no invalid executing message in any supernode's cross-safe chain, and the supernodes always agreed.

Limitations:
- The safety check reads each supernode's cross-safe head through its rollup RPC. It needs one EL per supernode per chain, so that it validates against the same chain view.
- `invalid-spam` only lands transactions when the sequencers' interop filter accepts invalid messages.

No effect on users; these are test tools. The repo's review agents were not run on this draft.

topPRs.title: op-reth!: drop the generics that only ever take one type
topPRs.author: joshklop
topPRs.body:
op-reth's crates carried type parameters that every caller, in this repo and in optimism-premium, fills with the same type. They make every bound and signature longer, suggest extension points no one uses, and stand in the way of the next step: turning op-reth into one concrete node with a small, tempo-style overrides API that optimism-premium can wrap instead of re-implementing op-reth's node and launch code.

This PR removes them in three commits, meant to be reviewed one at a time:

1. **EVM and payload stack** (`db294887a1`). `OpEvmConfig`, `OpBlockAssembler`, the payload builder and payload types, and the debug witness RPCs lose their chain spec, node primitives, receipt builder and payload-attributes parameters.
2. **Node, RPC, engine and consensus wiring** (`fbe3502e19`). `OpAddOns` becomes `OpAddOns<N>`; `OpEngineTypes`, `OpEngineValidator`, `OpEngineApi`, `OpBeaconConsensus`, `OpExecutionPayloadValidator` and `OpSdmAdminApi` lose their single-instantiation parameters; `OpFullNodeTypes` folds into `OpNodeTypes`.
3. **Payload transactions, txpool, storage and CLI** (`2bf0e403ab`). `OpPayloadBuilder`'s `Txs` hook and the `OpPayloadTransactions` trait go; `OpPooledTransaction` and `OpStorage` become concrete; `OpCustomTransactionPool` drops its blob-store parameter; `Cli`, `Commands`, `CliApp`, `InitStateCommandOp` and the `proofs` subcommands drop their chain spec parser and RPC validator parameters.

No effect on operators or chains: no RPC method, wire format, metric, flag or config key changes, and block building, execution and validation run the same code. Only the Rust API changes.

A few changes go slightly past removing parameters, because removing them made something else dead:
- `OpEngineTypes` moves into the payload crate and replaces `OpPayloadTypes`, which had an identical `PayloadTypes` impl. The RPC crate's `OpEngineApi` needs to name it, and the RPC crate cannot depend on the node crate.
- `OpEngineValidator` loses its provider, which only the hand-written `Clone` read.
- `OpAddOns::min_suggested_priority_fee` goes; the value still reaches the eth API through `OpEthApiBuilder`.
- The `engine-api-access` example goes: it only showed replacing the engine API builder, which `OpAddOns` no longer allows.
- The `priority` node test goes: it only exercised the removed payload-transactions hook.

Kept generic on purpose, because optimism-premium or op-reth-test-engine fills them with their own types: `OpEvmConfig`'s `EvmFactory`; `OpPayloadBuilder`'s `Pool`/`Client`/`Evm`; `OpPayloadBuilderCtx`'s `Evm`; `OpPoolBuilder`'s transaction type, ordering and validator wrapper; `DerivedPayloadServiceBuilder`'s service; `OpEthApi`'s node; `Cli`'s extension args; and the engine type on the `OpEngineApi` RPC trait (premium's in-process tests call `OpEngineApiClient::<OpEngineTypes>`). `OpEngineApi` keeps its `Validator` parameter because the validator type lives in the node crate, which the RPC crate cannot name.

optimism-premium compiles against this branch in ethereum-optimism/optimism-premium#493: its fallout is type-argument edits and one alias (`PremiumCli = Cli<PremiumCliArgs>`).

Reviews: rust-code-reviewer and deletion-reviewer ran on each commit. They found no behavior change. Applied: their leftover-docs and orphaned-dependency findings, and making the `proofs` subcommands concrete. Not taken: dropping the txpool transaction type parameters (premium's policy pool uses its own type), dropping the engine type from the `OpEngineApi` RPC trait (premium's tests use it), and a type alias for `OpEthApiBuilder`'s `EthApi`.

BREAKING CHANGE: Rust crates that build on op-reth must drop the removed type arguments and items:
- `OpEvmConfig<ChainSpec, N, R, EvmFactory>` is now `OpEvmConfig<EvmFactory>`, built for `OpChainSpec`, `OpPrimitives` and `OpRethReceiptBuilder`. `OpEvmConfig::new` is removed (use `OpEvmConfig::optimism`), and `new_with_evm_factory` no longer takes a receipt builder. Bound an EVM config by `NextBlockEnvCtx = OpNextBlockEnvAttributes` instead of `BuildNextEnv<...>`.
- `OpBlockAssembler`, `OpPayloadBuilderAttributes`, `OpBuiltPayload` and the `Attrs` parameter of `OpPayloadBuilderCtx`, `OpPayloadBuilder`, `OpDebugWitnessApi` and `DebugApiExt` are gone, as are the `OpPayloadPrimitives`, `OpAttributes` and `OpReplayNodePrimitives` traits and the unused `ExecutedPayload`. Read `OpPayloadBuilderAttributes`' public fields instead of the `OpAttributes` methods.
- `OpPayloadTypes` becomes `OpEngineTypes` (now in `reth-optimism-payload-builder`, still re-exported from `reth-optimism-node`), `OpFullNodeTypes` becomes `OpNodeTypes`, and `OpEngineValidator::new` takes only the chain spec. `OpAddOns::{with_engine_api, with_payload_validator, with_engine_validator, with_rpc_middleware}` and `OpAddOnsBuilder::with_rpc_middleware` are gone; a node that needs a different engine API or validator implements its own add-ons.
- `OpPayloadBuilder::with_transactions` and `OpPayloadTransactions` are gone: the payload builder always takes the pool's best transactions. `OpPooledTransaction` takes no type arguments, the unused `OpTransactionPool` alias is gone, `OpCustomTransactionPool<S, V, O>` is `OpCustomTransactionPool<V, O>`, and `OpPoolBuilder` only builds pools for nodes whose types are `OpNodeTypes`.
- `Cli<OpChainSpecParser, Args>` becomes `Cli<Args>`; `Commands`, `CliApp`, `InitStateCommandOp` and the `proofs` subcommands take no chain spec parser.

topPRs.title: op-node,op-alt-da: read L1 block transactions without decoding deposits
topPRs.author: sebastianst
topPRs.body:
An L3's L1 is an OP Stack chain: every L1 block starts with an L1-info deposit, and a batch can be force-included through a deposit. op-node's data sources and the alt-DA challenge processing decode all of an L1 block's transactions with go-ethereum, which works only on op-geth. On upstream go-ethereum (#24176) the decode fails on every such block and derivation stalls.

They now read the block's transactions as EIP-2718 bytes through the new `InfoAndRawTxsByHash` and decode each by its class:

- A deposit to the batch inbox from the batcher address is a batcher transaction, as op-geth's signer made it before by returning the deposit's `From`.
- A post-exec transaction never is.
- Anything else goes through `isValidBatchTx` unchanged.

A transaction that does not decode still fails the block with a temporary error. No chain's derivation changes. New tests feed a block shaped like an OP Stack block through the real L1 client into the calldata source, the blob source and the alt-DA challenge processing; on #24176 without this change they fail with `failed to decode tx 0: transaction type not supported`.

The L1 request-time metric's `method` label changes from `InfoAndTxsByHash` to `InfoAndRawTxsByHash`, and its time no longer includes decoding the transactions. The unused `node.L1Client` interface is removed.

kona does not derive from an OP Stack L1 either: its L1 providers decode with alloy's Ethereum transaction envelope. That is not changed here and is tracked in #24284.
